author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Teacher, Not a Verdict
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The apprentice arrived carrying a notebook filled with Severus Snape's heroic deeds.

That was not what they'd intended, of course. They believed they had compiled a respectful account of a complicated man. The fact that it sounded like an advertisement for sainthood had escaped them.

"My name is Orin," they said, offering a hand. "I'm studying historical testimony for the Moonroot oral-history program."

Severus looked at the notebook.

"How unfortunate."

Orin smiled nervously.

"I've read about your work during the war."

"Have you?"

"Yes. I think you were one of the greatest heroes of your generation."

The silence was extraordinary.

I was arranging copies of the Closed Bells report on the shelf. I stopped moving. From the corner of my eye, I saw Severus's expression settle into something very still.

"On what evidence?" he asked.

Orin opened the notebook.

"Well, you were a double agent. You protected students. You made sacrifices no one understood until afterward."

"And?"

"And you were misunderstood."

"Was I?"

Orin looked at me for help.

I set down the papers.

"Why don't you tell him which sources you used?"

They listed several popular histories, an article written shortly after the war, and a memoir by somebody who had met Severus twice. None of the material was wholly invented. Some of it was incomplete. All of it treated the ending as though it retroactively explained every choice that came before.

Severus took the notebook, with permission, and turned to the first page.

"Here you say I had no choice."

Orin nodded.

"That was the tragic part."

"No," he said. "That is the part you have mistaken."

The apprentice looked wounded.

Severus returned the notebook.

"I made choices. Some were constrained by threats. Some were made in ignorance. Others were wrong. If you remove my agency, you do not make me admirable. You make the harm inexplicable."

Orin swallowed.

"I didn't mean to insult you."

"You have not insulted me. You have made a bad argument."

I bit back a smile.

It wasn't a gentle conversation. But Severus was teaching, not sentencing. I could see him making an effort to leave the apprentice room to correct themself.

"Would you show me where it goes wrong?" Orin asked.

Severus looked surprised.

Then he pulled out a chair.

"Sit."

For the next hour, he took the notebook apart line by line.

He asked which claims had witnesses. Which were based on later interpretation. Which events had harmed people, regardless of his reasons. Where Orin had substituted an adjective for an explanation.

"Brave is not a substitute for precise," he said.

Orin wrote that down.

They worked without an audience until Neri came through the doorway to retrieve the ledger report. Neri paused, listened, and quietly continued to the other room.

I brought tea.

Severus accepted his cup without breaking the sentence he was explaining.

Orin drank theirs too quickly and burned their tongue.

"Careful," I said.

They winced.

Severus looked at the cup.

"An instructive example of consequences arriving before understanding."

I laughed.

Orin laughed too, after a moment.

By afternoon, the notebook had more corrections than original lines. Orin looked exhausted.

"Do you still think I should write the piece?" they asked.

"That depends on whether you intend to revise it."

"I do."

"Then write it."

"What should I call you?"

Severus considered.

"Someone who made choices and must answer for them."

"That's a terrible title."

"An honest one."

I watched Orin think.

"Maybe that's the point," they said.

Severus gave the smallest nod.

Before Orin went, Neri returned with a sealed paper sleeve.

"One of your references contains testimony given confidentially," they said. "You may document that a statement was received. You may not publish its contents."

Orin frowned. "But I need the detail to support my argument."

"Then you require a different argument," Severus said.

"How can I tell the truth if I leave things out?"

"By declining to steal someone else's truth."

The words landed harder than either of us expected. Severus stared at the papers in his hands. He had spent a lifetime knowing what secrets could cost, and he was trying not to turn that knowledge into another weapon.

Orin considered the sleeve. "Could I ask the witness?"

"If they can be approached without identifying them," Neri said. "And if you are ready to hear no."

Orin pulled the confidential quotation from the draft. We found two publicly available accounts that supported part of the chronology but not the detail they wanted to claim. Orin wrote UNKNOWN beside the unresolved date.

"People will think I didn't do my research," they said.

"Better that than pretending the evidence is complete," Severus answered.

I watched him turn the notebook toward the apprentice rather than reaching across to correct it himself.

"Your work must be yours," he said. "So must your mistakes."

Orin made the change in their own handwriting. Their paper was less flattering, much more difficult, and finally honest.


When the apprentice left, they took their notebook and a stack of primary-source references. No blessing. No grand declaration. Just work to do.

I was proud of Severus, but I waited until the archive was nearly empty before telling him.

"You didn't let them turn you into a monument," I said.

"I have never cared for statues."

"Toph would approve."

"That is a deeply unsettling endorsement."

I laughed.

Severus gathered the loose papers into a careful stack.

"Orin will probably write something foolish anyway," he said.

"Maybe. But they asked to learn. You gave them a way."

He looked down at his hands.

"I used to think teaching was the art of making students fear mistakes."

"And now?"

"Now I suspect it is the art of making them capable of recognizing one."

I stepped closer.

"That sounds suspiciously kind."

"Do not spread the rumor."

The evening light caught the edge of his hair. There were dark smudges of ink on his fingers, and he had forgotten to remove his outer robe after the morning's catalog work. I brushed a speck of dust from his shoulder.

He watched me.

"You're staring."

"Am I?"

"Yes."

"I like you."

"An alarming lapse of judgment."

"I've been making it for some time."

He tried to look severe. His mouth betrayed him.

I took his hand and led him toward the little reading nook behind the archive's west room. It was empty, quiet, and warm enough to escape the draft from the main hall.

Severus stopped beside the shelf.

"Jasper."

"Yes?"

"I had expected you to find the discussion tiresome."

"I found it difficult. That's not the same."

He looked at me.

"I know you have many people you care about, and I know we have agreed what that means for us. Sometimes I still wonder whether you'd rather spend your evenings with someone less complicated."

I felt a small ache in my chest.

"Severus, you're not a problem I agreed to solve. You're someone I choose. That doesn't require you to become easy."

He let out a slow breath.

"And if I remain profoundly unpleasant?"

"Then I'll tell you when you're being unpleasant."

"How romantic."

"Would you like a demonstration?"

His eyebrows rose.

I kissed him before he could find a better insult. He answered with a warmth that made me forget the smell of old paper for a moment. His fingers settled against my waist, asking without words whether I wanted him closer.

I did.

We stayed until the last lamp in the archive was turned down, then went home together. The evening was private and unhurried, the kind of intimacy that needed no witness or verdict.

The next morning, a note from Orin arrived at Moonroot.

They had rewritten the opening.

It began, not with an accusation or a hymn of praise, but with a question about the difference between what a person intended and what their choices did.

Severus read it and set it on the table.

"Better," he said.

I smiled.

For him, that was practically applause.
